title: Audio input and speech output
summary: Speech to text and text to speech are separate services with separate modes: live streaming, fast synchronous files and batch. Pick the mode by latency need, volume and the extras you need, such as speaker labels or word timestamps.
useIf: You turn audio into text for search, captions, analytics or an agent, or you speak a text answer back.
avoidIf: The user is in a live conversation and you want one model to listen and speak. See the realtime topic instead.

explain.md: **Transcription** has three delivery modes. *Live* audio (a call, a microphone) goes to a streaming service. *Files* go to a synchronous call that returns a transcript, sometimes faster than real time. *Large backlogs* go to an asynchronous batch service. Azure Speech names these real-time, fast transcription and batch transcription, and adds diarization (up to 35 speakers), phrase lists and custom speech [[tr4]].

On OpenAI's file endpoint (checked 2026-10-13) start with `gpt-transcribe` for recorded speech in its original language [[tr1]]. Files can be up to 25 MB in `mp3`, `mp4`, `mpeg`, `mpga`, `m4a`, `wav` or `webm`. Add context with `prompt`, `keywords` and `languages` (it replaces the singular `language`, so never send both). Keywords are hints, so check they do not make unspoken terms appear. Use `gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize` only for speaker labels (`diarized_json`, and `chunking_strategy` set for audio over 30 seconds). Use `whisper-1` for word timestamps or translation into English.

**Speech output** on OpenAI uses `gpt-4o-mini-tts`, which accepts `instructions` for tone, accent and speed. `tts-1` has lower latency and `tts-1-hd` higher quality. Audio streams over chunked transfer, and `wav` or `pcm` give the fastest response [[tr2]]. Policy requires telling users the voice is AI-generated. Azure offers over 600 standard voices across 150 or more locales through Voice Live [[r7]].

explain.title: Pick the transcription mode
explain.alt: Live audio goes to streaming transcription. Recorded audio needing an answer in seconds goes to fast transcription. Large backlogs go to batch.

explain.title: Check limits per deployment
explain.md: The 25 MB file limit is documented for OpenAI's endpoint. A one hour mp3 at 128 kbps is about 58 MB, so long recordings must be split or compressed, or sent to a batch service built for them.

whereToUse: Live captions for webinars and meetings (streaming)
Voicemail and short recordings that need a transcript within seconds (fast or file)
Call-centre archives and lecture libraries (batch, with diarization)
Voice assistants that read answers aloud with a steerable voice

use: Streaming when a person or agent reads the text while the audio is still arriving
Fast or file transcription when audio is complete and predictable latency matters
Batch when volume is large and nobody waits
avoid: File transcription in a loop of small chunks to fake live captions: latency and cost add up
Diarization models for ordinary transcription, since they are specialised
Synthetic voices with no disclosure to users
flips: Domain terms are mis-heard: add a phrase list or keywords and re-measure
Speaker labels needed: switch to a diarization-capable path and set chunking
A caller expects spoken replies in one second: move to realtime speech-to-speech

pitfalls.symptom: Brand names and codes are transcribed wrongly
pitfalls.fix: Add `prompt`, `keywords` or a phrase list, then measure that spoken terms improve and unspoken ones do not appear.

pitfalls.cause: Both `language` and `languages` were sent, or a code was unsupported
pitfalls.fix: With `gpt-transcribe` send only `languages`, and use supported codes.

pitfalls.cause: The file exceeds the 25 MB limit
pitfalls.fix: Compress, split on silence, or use a batch service.

pitfalls.symptom: Diarization of a long meeting fails or gives unusable segments
pitfalls.cause: The docs require `chunking_strategy` for audio over 30 seconds and it was omitted
pitfalls.fix: Set `chunking_strategy` to `auto` or a voice activity configuration.

scenarios.title: Archive of 5,000 hours
scenarios.situation: A company needs transcripts of years of recorded support calls, with speaker labels, for analytics. Nobody is waiting on any single file.
scenarios.question: Which mode do you use?

options.name: Batch transcription with diarization
options.why: Batch is built for large volumes of recorded files and supports diarization [[tr4]].
options.tradeoff: Asynchronous: results arrive later and you manage jobs.

options.name: Fast transcription per file
options.tradeoff: Fine for moderate volume, but you manage concurrency and file limits yourself.

options.name: Realtime speech-to-speech replay
options.why: It is a conversation engine and bills audio tokens for a growing session.
options.tradeoff: Right only when a live caller needs spoken answers.

flips.if: A supervisor needs results within seconds of the call ending
flips.then: Use fast transcription for new calls and batch for the backlog.

flips.if: Only a keyword search is needed

scenarios.takeaway: Large, patient workloads belong in batch.

scenarios.title: Live captions for a webinar
scenarios.situation: A platform shows captions during webinars with thousands of attendees. Captions must appear within a second or two of speech.
unknowns: Is there a caption accuracy target?
scenarios.question: What do you use?

options.name: Streaming transcription (real-time speech to text)
options.why: It returns intermediate results as audio arrives, which live captions need [[tr4]].
options.tradeoff: Partial text is revised, so the interface must handle updates.

options.name: File transcription of 10-second chunks
options.why: Chunking adds delay, breaks words at boundaries and multiplies calls.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for delayed captions where a lag of tens of seconds is fine.

options.name: Batch transcription after the event
options.why: Cheap and accurate for the recording.
options.tradeoff: Gives no live captions, so use it for the on-demand replay only.

flips.if: Captions may lag by half a minute

flips.then: Add phrase lists or custom speech.

scenarios.takeaway: Live text needs a streaming path.

quiz.q: OpenAI's file transcription limit is 25 MB. About how many minutes of 128 kbps mp3 audio fit in one file?
quiz.explain: 128 kbps is 16 KB per second. 25 MB divided by 16 KB is about 1,560 seconds, roughly 26 minutes. Binary megabytes give about 27 minutes, inside the tolerance.

quiz.q: A diarization request for a 40-minute meeting is misbehaving. Which setting does the documentation require for audio longer than 30 seconds?
options: `chunking_strategy` set to `auto` or a voice activity configuration
quiz.explain: The diarization guide requires `chunking_strategy` for audio over 30 seconds. An output format name, keywords and a TTS model do not address it.

quiz.q: Which are reasons to choose batch over streaming transcription?
options: Volume is large and nobody waits
You need captions during a live event
Intermediate results must reach an agent mid-call
quiz.explain: Recorded audio at volume suits asynchronous jobs. Live captions and mid-call assist need streaming.

flashcards.front: Name the three speech-to-text delivery modes in Azure Speech.
flashcards.back: Real-time (streaming with intermediate results), fast transcription (synchronous files, faster than real time), and batch (asynchronous, large volumes).
Only when you need speaker labels. Request `diarized_json` and set `chunking_strategy` for audio longer than 30 seconds.

flashcards.front: Which TTS output formats give the fastest response on OpenAI?
flashcards.back: `wav` or `pcm`. The default is `mp3`, and audio can stream as it is generated.
